The single-vineyard wines from Chimney Rock are particularly definitive.

Cliff Lede.zin: ‘It was a lower-yielding vintage,’ noted Christopher Tynan, Director of Winemaking for Cliff Lede Vineyards, who emphasised that the quality of the 2021 harvest in Stags Leap was exceptional.

Corison.zin: That’s “cool” in Napa.’ Cathy Corison also recalls the atypical summer.
When I started making the Corison Cabernets, there were no sub-AVAs.

Dalla Valle Vineyards.zin: Dalla Valle Vineyards Maya, Napa Valley (Oakville) Right out of the gate, at the cork’s pull, it is medium-bodied and so approachable in 2022.

Grace Family Vineyards.zin: Grace Family Vineyards Reliquus Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley (St Helena) Reliquus is crafted from a blend of fruit sourced from Grace Family’s estate vineyards in the St.

Inglenook.zin: Yet at Francis Ford Coppola’s Inglenook, in the warmer, flatter Rutherford AVA, winemaker Chris Phelps had all his Cabernet Sauvignon fruit in the cellar by 24 September.
The standouts of the tasting for me are The Armagh Shiraz 2016, Inglenook Rubicon 2017, Galatrona Petrolo 2018 and Bibi Graetz’s toweringly good Tastamatta 2018.

La Jota.zin: Napa Valley Cabernet: Full 2018 vintage report Winemaker for Lokoya and La Jota, Chris Carpenter describes Howell Mountain as having a ‘gravely minerality that comes through, and a mid-palate that none of the mountain wines from the Mayacamas come close to.

Lithology.zin: ‘If you look before the heatwave,’ says Lithology winemaker Matt Sands, ‘it was a great growing season – healthy canopies, excellent fruit set and well-sized berries.’ But the heat came and panic set in.

Matthiasson.zin: Their 2014 Matthiasson Cabernet Sauvignon Napa Valley was among my top-scoring wines with 96-points.

Merryvale.zin: Corison, Merryvale, Spottswoode and Hourglass’ Estate bottlings are particularly classic examples of this diverse region.

Paul Hobbs.zin: Paul Hobbs Cuvee Sophia Proprietary Red, Napa Valley (Coombsville) Perhaps the most approachable at the pull of the cork this wine will ever be, with plenty of tannins for potential cellaring, but really, it is accessible early on.

Pilcrow.zin: Pilcrow’s Jonah Beer says: ‘Mother Nature allowed us to walk through the vintage rather than sprint.

Pride Mountain Vineyards.zin: ‘We had some issues, but the wines are pure, unctuous and give immediate satisfaction.’ Sonoma County Pride Mountain Vineyards winemaker Sally Johnson has a unique perch in the Mayacamas Mountains that separate Sonoma and Napa counties.

Shafer.zin: Shafer winemaker Elias Fernandez said that with longer hang times and a perfect growing season, ‘the fruit looked phenomenal’.
Shafer produces more modern iterations, and Realm Cellars takes this profile to bonafide ‘cult’ status.

Spring Mountain Vineyard.zin: That awareness, coupled with the devastation of the native forest land on the Spring Mountain Vineyard estate, could mean Napa County will permit them to plant more hectares where vines had never been planted—possibly an additional 36ha.
My five-decade tasting confirmed that the wines of Spring Mountain Vineyard are real treasures of Napa—meant for enjoyment now and, as we will see—later.

The Vice.zin: The Vice Batch #142 Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley It is a well-structured, food-friendly wine with depth and approachability.

Turnbull.zin: Turnbull’s Black Label and Groth’s Reserve are solid examples.

Ata Rangi.zin: Ata Rangi first achieved full organic certification for two of its vineyards, McCrone and Home Block, in 2014, with the rest following soon after, and is also unusual in New Zealand in that a large percentage of its vines remain on their own roots.
Widely regarded as one of New Zealand’s best wineries, Ata Rangi’s stylish, complex Pinot Noirs have a solid track record for ageing beautifully.

Felton Road.zin: That is the story of Nigel Greening, British-born owner of Felton Road in Central Otago, New Zealand, who just celebrated his 25th vintage.
He says ‘Felton Road lives in these two halves, before and after.’ The wines clearly have more tension and ageability now.

Wild Irishman.zin: Shaw of Wild Irishman notes: ‘Alexandra is the hottest and coldest place in New Zealand – it is very continental.’ The dramatic temperature shifts here see the highest day and coldest night temperatures.

Schloss Gobelsburg.zin: Today Schloss Gobelsburg produces over forty wines in a range of styles, but its most esteemed wine is the Riesling from Zöbinger Heiligenstein.
See tasting notes of 17 Schloss Gobelsburg Heiligenstein Rieslings Wines are listed in score order.

00 Wines.zin: The grapes for 00 Wines come from the ‘H Block’ on the north side of the property that Dominique and Tarlov planted, with both Dijon clones from Burgundy and older Wente clones from U.C.
The quest that truly motivates 00 Wines is to produce Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from the world’s greatest cool-climate sites.

Arterberry Maresh.zin: His Arterberry Maresh Dundee Hills Pinot Noir (96-points) is only $33.50.

Bergström.zin: The Bergström approach is based on biodynamic and regenerative farming in the vineyards and crafting vineyard and single-block bottlings that give their wines a real sense of place.
He and his wife Karen Bergström both had successful medical careers and sought a family legacy that was a return to John’s farming roots.

Bethel Heights.zin: The conditions, together with the rising tide of Chardonnay in the valley, delivered the first 100-point wine from Oregon in Decanter ’s history: Bethel Heights, The High Wire Chardonnay 2023, a simply mesmerising wine from own-rooted Wente clone vines planted in 1977.
The 48-year-old, own-rooted Chardonnay vines that are behind Bethel Heights’ 100-point The High Wire Chardonnay.

Cimento.zin: ‘You had to have people in the rows,’ says David Wanek, proprietor of Cimento in The Rocks District, ‘and if you didn’t, you can have variability.

Composition.zin: Credit: Composition A French icon’s Oregon roots In 1995, a young Bertrand de Villaine was a college business student who accepted a one-semester exchange programme at Linfield University in McMinnville, Oregon.

Delmas.zin: ‘2021 was an interesting vintage,’ says Brooke Delmas Robertson, director of viticulture and winemaking for Delmas in The Rocks District AVA.

Domaine Drouhin.zin: For the Domaine Drouhin bottling, the malolactic fermentation is blocked for the tank-fermented portion so that the wine retains a vibrant freshness.
Domaine Drouhin Véronique Drouhin was one of the original Burgundian pioneers of the Willamette Valley, arriving in 1986.

Evening Land.zin: Evening Land Initially planted in 1984 with own-rooted vines, Evening Land has been considerably retooled by sommelier Raj Parr, winemaker Sashi Moorman and their partners.

Evesham Wood.zin: When he started Evesham Wood, he keenly remembered his retail roots, focusing on producing wines he could afford to buy and drink regularly,’ says Nuccio.

Eyrie Vineyards.zin: Eyrie Vineyards Eyrie Vineyards is the legacy brand for the Dundee Hills, the Willamette Valley and really all of the Pacific Northwest.
In many ways, the wines of Eyrie Vineyards are historic in their own right; these bottles represent the beginning of it all.

Lingua Franca.zin: Lingua Franca Master Sommelier Larry Stone has set up shop across the street from Evening Land in Eola-Amity Hills.

Walter Scott.zin: A former student of sommelier Erica Landon (who founded Walter Scott with her husband Ken Pahlow), he has worked with some of the greatest names in Oregon, and at Domaine de Montille in Meursault with winemaker Brian Sieve.
Among his early devotees was Ken Pahlow (pictured, above), whose Walter Scott label now produces some of the valley’s top Chardonnays every vintage.

Albino Rocca.zin: That said, one of my top wines – Albino Rocca’s gorgeous Ronchi – is located on the village’s eastern flank.

Aldo Conterno.zin: Giacomo Conterno of the Aldo Conterno estate noted: ‘The Nebbiolo was beautifully ripe but one had to avoid excessive ripeness that could give cooked aromas and flavours.
Tasted earlier this year, Aldo Conterno’s Cicala is a wonderfully evocative rendering.

Antoniolo.zin: Antoniolo has also been making consistently solid wines in recent decades, and the family’s Osso San Grato site stands alongside the greatest crus of the Langhe.

Azelia.zin: Azelia has just launched a new bottling from Cerretta, both Luigi Einaudi and Scarpa have a Monvigliero on the horizon and Francesco Rinaldi will release a Rocche dell’Annunziata starting with the 2018 vintage.

Azelia’s Voghera Riserva (in bond £87.50 Berry Bros & Rudd) and Ceretto’s Cannubi San Lorenzo (in bond £919-£945/magnum Crop & Vine, Ideal Wine Co, VinQuinn) made a strong case for old vines in difficult years.

Bartolo Mascarello.zin: A phenomenon more often seen during the height of the summer, Maria-Teresa Mascarello at Bartolo Mascarello, in the Barolo township, recalls that, ‘we harvested in the dust.
Top three Barolo classico 2016 picks: Bartolo Mascarello, Barolo 2016: A co-fermentation of multiple plots, this ageworthy Barolo is a classic in the truest sense.

Borgogno.zin: Earlier this year, Borgogno’s Riserva was the highlight at a 10-year release retrospective.

Brezza.zin: Top producers As for individual producers, this is not the first time that a wine from Brezza comes out on top in a Decanter panel tasting, and I dare say it won’t be the last either.
Enzo Brezza has transformed this estate, introducing organic methods to realise the full potential of some excellently sited vineyards.

Bruno Giacosa.zin: Ratcheting it up a few notches, Bruno Giacosa and Sandrone’s bottlings from the Valmaggiore cru were two of my top picks of the entire report.
Bruno Giacosa, Barolo Falletto: Innate refinement is already evident here but delaying gratification will vastly improve enjoyment.

Castello di Verduno.zin: Castello di Verduno, Barolo: A flagbearer for the village of Verduno; as accessible in price as it is in drinkability.

Ceretto.zin: In terms of personal preferences, Ceretto’s Brunate was among my favourites for its sheer, undemanding drinking pleasure.

Domenico Clerico.zin: Prime examples are E Pira & Figli’s’ Mosconi and Domenico Clerico’s Ciabot Mentin Ginestra.
Nephew of the late Domenico Clerico, he made his first Barolo in 2020 when he was just 17.

E Pira & Figli.zin: ‘I was in full experimental mode,’ recalls E Pira & Figli’s Chiara Boschis of the 1996 vintage.

Elio Altare.zin: Elio Altare, Vigna Bricco, Barolo Cerretta: The innate balance is already palpable here, promising harmonious ageing.

Elvio Cogno.zin: As Valter Fissore at Elvio Cogno states: ‘It is supposed to be a friendly wine for drinking chilled in the summer.’ He purchased a vineyard outside the DOCG zone specifically for Langhe Nebbiolo and the 2023 Montegrilli is a deliciously fruity and crisp Nebbiolo.

Ettore Germano.zin: Ettore Germano, Cerretta 2008 Sergio Germano’s favourite Barolo from his portfolio is the quintessence of Serralunga – power and intensity without being heavy, with a shock of electric energy to balance the concentration and depth.
Ettore Germano, Cerretta 2008 Serralunga is packed with good producers, and Sergio Germano is among them (terrific Riesling too).

Fletcher.zin: While the latter is clearly Fletcher’s calling card, he also succeeds with a characterful Arneis, Pinot-esque Langhe Nebbiolo, and a partial whole-cluster Barbera.
Fletcher resigned from Ceretto earlier this year but is extremely deferential.

Fontanafredda.zin: What Barolo Riserva 2019 to drink when Green light: Over the next 10 years Fontanafredda, Barolo Riserva: This classic blend of historic vineyards is settling into its groove.

Fratelli Alessandria.zin: Others, such as Fratelli Alessandria’s Monvigliero were evolving more harmoniously.

GB Burlotto.zin: At GB Burlotto in Verduno, the estate’s Barolo Monvigliero spent 33 months ageing in large oak barrels – a sign of the vintage’s quality, according to fifth-generation winemaker Fabio Alessandria.
GB Burlotto’s newest bottling has garnered attention for the MGA, but 2021 offers many convincing efforts including those from Sara Vezza and Fortemasso.

GD Vajra.zin: GD Vajra, Albe, Barolo: When ‘young vines’ means three decades in the ground… This is much more than just a straightforward ‘entry’ Barolo.

Giacomo Conterno.zin: And, as prices were already soaring for the three ‘big Gs’ – Giacomo Conterno, Bruno Giacosa and Gaja – aficionados started seeking out treasures among (then) lesser-known estates such as Cavallotto, GD Vajra and GB Burlotto: all highly regarded today.
However, despite coming from the mediocre 1987 vintage, Giacomo Conterno’s Monfortino Barolo Riserva made a lasting impression.

Gian Luca Colombo.zin: Gian Luca Colombo’s Meretto is another must-try if you can find it.

Giuseppe Cortese.zin: Bruno Giacosa and Ca’ del Baio in the former, and Giuseppe Cortese in the latter are among my top picks.

Giuseppe Rinaldi.zin: Carlotta Rinaldi at Giuseppe Rinaldi acknowledges that they could make a separate Ravera bottling, ‘but we don’t feel it is harmonious on its own,’ she explains.
Besides top picks such as Aldo Conterno’s Colonnello and Giuseppe Rinaldi’s bottling, the lesser-known Cascina Amalia and Marrone are worth seeking out.

La Barbatella.zin: Produced since 1983, La Barbatella is a benchmark for unoaked Barbera d’Asti.

La Gironda.zin: La Gironda, Oddero and Olim Bauda are names to look for here.

Luigi Pira.zin: There were excellent wines made in all the various crus and townships – another plus.’ Luigi Pira, Marenca 2009 A Serralunga d’Alba Barolo that is slightly more approachable than most, given the tough-as-nails tannins this area is known for.

Margherita Otto.zin: This is the model he emulates for his own Barolo Margherita Otto, which he started making commercially in 2015.

Mauro Molino.zin: Mauro Molino, Barolo: Despite a pinch from Monforte, this is so elegantly La Morra-esque.

Mauro Veglio.zin: Mauro Veglio, Barolo Riserva Rocche dell’Annunziata: Barrique ageing has already softened the tannins in this seductively styled Riserva.

Monte Maletto.zin: A new generation is braving the elements, too, with boutique projects – one, Monte Maletto, captures the alpine character and delicacy of Carema.

Muraje.zin: Deborah and Federico Santini of Muraje are emblematic of the fresh young faces that are reversing years of viticultural abandonment.

Oddero.zin: In terms of quantity, a lot of producers are releasing still-older Riserva: Oddero’s Vignarionda 2014, Domenico Clerico’s PerCristina 2011, Parusso’s Oro 2000.
The 20-year club Oddero, Barolo Riserva Vignarionda: Properly austere without being severe, it is a masterful example of vintage and site.

Paitin.zin: Paitin, Sorì Paitin Vecchie Vigne, Barbaresco Serraboella: Its signature austerity is just sufficiently curbed without sacrificing longevity.

Palladino.zin: Palladino, Barolo Serralunga d’Alba: One of the most consistent village bottlings that is so satisfyingly Serralunga.

Produttori del Barbaresco.zin: Conversely, Produttori del Barbaresco’s bottling was a stunning demonstration.

Prunotto.zin: Prunotto’s winemaker Gianluca Torrengo reports that ‘while in Barolo there were 90-100mm of rain, only 40mm fell in Barbaresco’, and furthermore, ‘in an area ranging from Cannubi [Barolo commune] to Fontanafredda [4km to its northeast], there was also hail’.
Yellow light: No rush, enjoy over the next 15 years Prunotto, Vigna Colonnello, Barolo Riserva Bussia: Personality wins over sheer force, but this is not lacking in backbone.

Sandrone.zin: I was also charmed by Luciano Sandrone’s Le Vigne, the most gorgeously textured and perfumed wine on the table.

Stefano Occhetti.zin: Stefano Occhetti is an excellent example of this new generation.

Tenuta Santa Caterina.zin: He purchased the derelict Tenuta Santa Caterina and has restored it to its former glory.

Tibaldi.zin: Daniela Tibaldi is one of a number of producers, however, who believes that 2016 will be even better.

Travaglini.zin: Travaglini’s Coste della Sesia is a beautiful snapshot of the fine-boned, fragrant expression of Nebbiolo found in north Piedmont’s cool, sub-alpine reaches.

Vietti.zin: Krause has handed the management of Vietti to its former owner Luca Currado to ensure continuity, while Réva and Castello di Perno have turned to Gianluca Colombo, who perfectly represents the link between advancing innovation and tradition.
Read Michaela’s full report on Barolo 2021 Barolo 2021: Top value picks Vietti, Barolo: While not actually the least expensive Barolo, what it delivers for the money is exceptional.

Azores Wine Company.zin: Farming around 100ha has not eclipsed Azores Wine Company’s desire to single out special vineyards, including Vinha dos Utras.

Casa da Passarella.zin: Exceptionally mineral, nuanced wines, skilfully made with zero or minimal added sulphur Casa da Passarella Conceived on a grand scale, this late 19th century Serra da Estrela estate was planted to 200ha (of which 40ha remain) by Amand d’Oliveira, who made his fortune in Brazil.
Like Porta dos Cavaleiros, my Casa da Passarella and MOB recommendations (see below) are old field blends, whole-bunch fermented and released with bottle age.

Herdade do Rocim.zin: Aged in both talha and French oak, Herdade do Rocim Vinha Micaela 2018 conforms more closely to the classical fine wine paradigm.

Niepoort.zin: ‘I don’t like fruitiness, I prefer the opposite – shyer, less easy, like me,’ says the former Niepoort winemaker, and indeed his elegant Dão field blend is no blockbuster.
Cement is making a comeback, used by Madeira, Raposo and Niepoort, who acquired Quinta da Lomba in 2012.

Clos Mogador.zin: René Barbier IV (born in 1973 in Nancy in France, home to his mother, Isabelle Meyer) is now at the wheel of Clos Mogador, the winery – one of the most celebrated in the region – founded by his father.

Gramona.zin: The cousins – sons, respectively, of Xavier and Jaume Gramona (cousins themselves) – are the sixth generation to take the reins of the storied Penedès winery, whose origins go back to the 1850s.
The cousins were therefore challenged to join Gramona and become acquainted with its operations and ethos in the hope of one day taking up the batons from their respective fathers.

Terroir al Límit.zin: It was at Mas Martinet that Huber first met South African winemaker Eben Sadie, with whom he first created Terroir al Límit in 2001, using fruit purchased from the Pérez family (Sadie has since moved back to Swartland to focus on his own project).
It’s worth noting that both Mas Martinet and Terroir al Límit use an element of reductive winemaking for added tension in the wines.

Torres.zin: Miquel explains: ‘A consumer in the UK knows Viña Sol, not Torres.’ I am not sure he is right, because the remarkable thing about those wines is the Torres brand reassurance of consistency and consistent improvement in quality and style.

The work has been going on long enough that Torres can now release finished wines, most recently Forcada (white); with Moneu appearing at the end of the year in a red blend, and Pirene, a high-altitude red coming soon.

Château Bellini.zin: He is currently restructuring and re-planting his new estate, Château Bellini, formerly Domaine de Fontlade, outside of Brignoles, and he even introduced his friend George Clooney to a neighbouring estate.

A great lover of art and opera, Bove renamed this domaine Château Bellini, after the opera composer Vincenzo Bellini and the Venetian painter Giovanni Bellini (he had already named his dog Bellini, too).

Château Canadel.zin: Others, namely Château Canadel and Peyraud’s Domaine Tempier, have a more traditional, intense tannic structure.

Château Galoupet.zin: The few exceptions among the cru classé estates are Clos Cibonne, Château Galoupet, and the top wines of Château St-Martin and Château St-Maur.
The Château Galoupet cru classé rosé comes in a 70% recycled glass bottle, which has a feuille morte colour.

Château Sainte Marguerite.zin: Giron added that the range of Château Sainte Marguerite wines will evolve, rather than grow in total volume, and over the next two years there will be a complete redesign of the range.

Château Ste Roseline.zin: Château Ste Roseline is as much visited for its 12th century abbey, the mummified remains of Ste Roseline and its contemporary art collection as for its wine.
One of Kylie Minogue’s rosé wines, made at Château Ste Roseline, is a cru classé.

Château Vignelaure.zin: Eloi Dürrbach, who made the wine at Château Vignelaure and then set up his own estate, Domaine de Trévallon, continued to make an equal blend of Cabernet and Syrah under the IGP Bouches-du-Rhône.

Château de Pibarnon.zin: L’Irreductble is a serious, unoaked, dark pink-red, while Eric de St Victor of Château de Pibarnon, recognising that Mourvèdre rosé takes time to open up, ages his Nuances in stoneware which gives tension and purity, before releasing the wine with a year’s age.
Château de Pibarnon’s Nuances and Bégude’s l’Irreductible are both almost entirely Mourvèdre.

Domaine Tempier.zin: It certainly seems criminal to shout about drinking Domaine Tempier’s rosé as soon as it is launched when it ages so splendidly.

Domaine de la Font des Pères.zin: Most producers use large old foudres, but a few are using new oak such as Château Vannières and Domaine de la Font des Pères whose wines have a modern, almost New World appeal, while the presence of Cinsault in a blend adds vivacity.

Cave de Tain.zin: None of the wines were deceased, though the Cave de Tain Classique was beginning to tire and arguably would have been better a few years ago.
And don’t forget Hermitage Vin de Paille – the Cave de Tain 1989 is still delicious, combining kaleidoscopic aromatics with perfect balance.

Domaine Belle.zin: More delicate wines, such as Domaine Belle’s Hermitage and Pierre-Jean Villa’s Côte-Rôtie Fongeant, were scored at 95 or 96 points by one or two judges but not all.

Domaine Clape.zin: The Domaine Gonon Saint Joseph rouge 2008 is lean but fresh and appetising, and Domaine Clape Cornas 2008 lacks a little of its characteristic intensity but is nonetheless complex, with peppery herbal aromatics.
There was room for a couple of top-scoring reds though, notably two 2010 Cornas from Domaine Clape and Vincent Paris, which are among Walls’s favourite vintages from that appellation to drink now.

Domaine Gonon.zin: He prefers his 2018s, an excellent vintage for Domaine Gonon, which are more elegant in style.

Domaine Guy Farge.zin: Value picks Ferraton ‘Les Grands Mûriers’ Cornas 2018 Domaine Guy Farge ‘Harmonie’ Cornas 2018 Domaine Mucyn ‘Aquilon’ Cornas 2018 Saint-Péray Hot vintages are rarely the most exciting for white wines in the Rhône; the last truly compelling vintage for whites was 2014.

Domaine JL Chave.zin: ‘It was the great terroirs that made good wines in 2021,’ said Jean-Louis Chave of Domaine JL Chave, ‘you needed slopes and old vines.’ This helped to avoid dilution, because rain runs off the slopes.
Whilst I wouldn’t have wanted to open the Domaine JL Chave much before now, the other bottles of red Hermitage would all have provided a lot of pleasure before today.

Domaine Laurent Habrard.zin: I’ve been enjoying Domaine Laurent Habrard’s exceptional Crozes-Hermitage rouge ‘Kévin’ that has retained a sense of freshness despite the dry conditions.

Domaine Lionnet.zin: ‘It was easy to manage in the vineyard,’ says Ludovic Izerable of Domaine Lionnet, who has vineyards in the southern part of the appellation near Cornas.

Domaine Marc Sorrel.zin: According to Guillaume Sorrel of Domaine Marc Sorrel, 30mm of rain was forecast, but over 100mm fell.

Domaine Niero.zin: Domaine Niero in particular made some fantastic wines in 2018, as did Domaine de Monteillet.

Domaine Rostaing.zin: Pierre Rostaing at Domaine Rostaing describes his 2017s as ‘structured, dense, with good concentration – all we needed to make good wines for the cellar.’ Compared to the 2015 vintage, 2017 is just as ripe, but more savoury and occasionally a little darker in fruit.
According to Pierre Rostaing of Domaine Rostaing, mildew can give earthy, bitter notes to a wine, so careful sorting was required.

Domaine Yann Chave.zin: Domaine Monier-Parréol Saint-Joseph rouge ‘Le Châtelet’ 2012 is in a lovely state of maturity now, and in Hermitage, the Domaine Yann Chave 2012 is just starting to come around, though will benefit from longer in bottle.

Domaine des Martinelles.zin: Hermitage is largely ready to be broached now, with wines such as Domaine des Martinelles old vine cuvée ‘Louis et Aimé’ now fully mature but still brimming with sap and intensity.

Domaine du Mortier.zin: At the lighter end of the scale, Domaine du Mortier ‘Bara’ is fresh and approachable; Ferraton’s ‘Paradis’ is fuller in body, but its bright aromatics are irresistible now.

M Chapoutier.zin: The outlier is M Chapoutier’s De L’Orée Ermitage Blanc, which I tasted alongside Michel Chapoutier at the Decanter Fine Wine Encounter event in New York in June last year.
M Chapoutier’s white Hermitage L’Ermite is a fine showing from the tricky and varied 2024 vintage, which you can read about in our extensive en primeur coverage.

Stéphane Ogier.zin: In fact, Stéphane Ogier won’t be making his single-vineyard Côte-Rôties this year; ‘It’s a fresher vintage,’ he says, ‘and they have their place.’ Yields were very varied even within individual parcels, and several estates said they had to chaptalise.

Stéphane Ogier, of his eponymous domaine, notes that ripening issues were more common with younger vines, and stressed the importance of fermenting with stems in 2022, which contributes structure and freshness and reduces alcohol levels.

Xavier Gérard.zin: I’m greatly enjoying Domaine Xavier Gérard’s 2017 Côte-Rôtie at the moment, and even the 2017 Domaine Jamet Côte-Rôtie is still vividly expressive, though it will be even better in 10 years time.

Château Rayas.zin: Château Rayas is indeed a Châteauneuf, but it bears little resemblance to other wines made in the appellation.
Château Rayas makes a richly textured white Châteauneuf from 50% Clairette, 50% Grenache Blanc.

Château de Beaucastel.zin: ‘We are no longer in the era of extraction,’ says François Perrin of Château de Beaucastel; ‘we’re in the era of elegance – but our elegance.’ Contemporary Châteauneuf still has a big frame, but it has lost weight and its tailoring is sharper.
The best wines of Châteauneuf such as Château de Beaucastel’s ‘Hommage à Jacques Perrin’ are deliciously harmonious now, and will continue to age well for another decade, if not more.

Château de Fonsalette.zin: Rayas, Pignan and Château de Fonsalette are all made at Rayas; any barrels deemed unsuitable for these cuvées are blended together to make La Pialade.
Perfecting the blend: Château de Fonsalette The Château de Fonsalette wines tasted at Matt Walls’ November 2025 tasting.

Clos des Papes.zin: ‘It happened in one night,’ says Vincent Avril of Clos des Papes who eventually lost 70% of his crop.
And Vincent Avril of Clos des Papes was impressed by the Bourboulenc and Piquepoul Blanc.

Clos du Mont-Olivet.zin: Châteauneuf-du-Pape, particularly the heavily Grenache-based wines from Clos du Mont-Olivet, Marcoux and Rayas, was perhaps the easiest to recognise with the pale hue, sweet fruit and structure.
The Châteauneuf-du-Pape wines all retail at more than €50, except for Clos du Mont-Olivet, while Château Rayas is around €700-a-bottle and Beaucastel Hommage à Jacques Perrin at €480.

Domaine Brusset.zin: Domaine Brusset’s Les Hauts de Montmirail was excellent, however.

Domaine Chamfort.zin: Aside from that, ‘2020 was a fairly easy year,’ says Vasco Perdigao of Domaine Chamfort, ‘even if “easy” years don’t really exist!’ The summer was very hot with the occasional rain shower, but cool nights helped to give the vines some respite.

Domaine Font de Michelle.zin: Guillaume Gonnet of Domaine Font de Michelle and his own eponymous label says: ‘In 10 years I haven’t planted any Grenache,’ instead replanting Mourvèdre, Counoise, Clairette and Bourboulenc.

Domaine Juliette Avril.zin: Domaine Juliette Avril An estate that’s been going from strength to strength over the past five years, Domaine Juliette Avril made some excellent red Châteauneufs in 2024, from its tradition bottling all the way up to its cuvées spéciales.

Domaine Le Sang des Cailloux.zin: Frédéri Férigoule of Domaine Le Sang des Cailloux stressed the importance of green harvesting in 2022: ‘We had a good crop load, but it was too much to ripen,’ he says.

Domaine Les Goubert.zin: Domaine Les Goubert’s Cuvée Florence and the ever-dependable Domaine Santa Duc’s Les Hautes Garrigues were both show-stoppers.

Domaine Lombard.zin: And a Domaine Lombard Brézème blanc 2008 tasted recently was a revelation, brimming with citrusy acidity, lavender honey and violets: a wine of extraordinary character.

Domaine Raspail-Ay.zin: In comparison the Domaine Raspail-Ay is comfortably mature and drinking beautifully.

Domaine Saint Gayan.zin: The 1998 Domaine Saint Gayan was particularly enjoyable, however; a wine to sink into like an old leather armchair.

Domaine de la Janasse.zin: That being said we were all on song for, respectively, the Domaine de la Janasse and Tardieu-Laurent Vieilles Vignes, as well as Domaine Peyre Rose (a top scoring wine in 2019 as well), but missed the reserved presence of Château de Beaucastel’s Hommage à Jacques Perrin.

Domaine de la Vieille Julienne.zin: Some winemakers I spoke to, such as Jean-Paul Daumen of Domaine de la Vieille Julienne and Jean-Louis Chave, believe this is evidence of vines adapting to an increasingly extreme climate.

Domaine des Bosquets.zin: A standout producer this year is Julien Brechet of Domaine des Bosquets and he describes 2024 as ‘a very honest vintage,’ meaning that it’s highly expressive of terroir, detailed and precise.
Reds are particularly fine, well-balanced and harmonious now; Domaine des Bosquets and Château Rayas were both in a particularly satisfying state of maturity last year.

Domaine des Escaravailles.zin: Madeline Ferran of Domaine des Escaravailles remembers ‘an ideal vintage, as much in the vineyard as the cellar.’ ‘Despite a complicated year due to Covid, nature spoiled us,’ she says.

Domaine du Cayron.zin: ‘One of my favourite vintages,’ says Delphine Faraud of Domaine du Cayron, who counts 1985, 1978 and 1971 as exceptional older years.

Le Vieux Donjon.zin: Southern Rhône 2019 wine of the vintage: Le Vieux Donjon, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Rhône, 2019 So how hot was it, exactly?

Mas de Boislauzon.zin: In Châteauneuf, all the wines of Mas de Boislauzon are in a good place, as is Clos des Papes.

Moulin de la Gardette.zin: In the south, Gigondas fared well (for producers such as Moulin de la Gardette, Domaine Les Semelles de Vent, and Mas des Restanques); some Châteauneufs were also very good (from Clos des Papes, Rotem & Mounir Saouma, and Henri Bonneau).

Pierre Amadieu.zin: Pierre Amadieu explains that it was an underrated year, characterised by its ‘extremely clean fruit, contrasting with the big and powerful 1998’.

Francisco Barona.zin: Among the top-scoring wines was Francisco Barona’s Finca Las Dueñas – a Reserva like no other, of robust, nuanced elegance, as charismatic as Barona himself.

Alonso & Pedrajo.zin: The stylistic range – from CVNE’s Monopole Clásico GR to Alonso & Pedrajo’s Suañé, via Ostatu’s Lore and Conde Valdemar’s Finca Alto Cantabria – is wide but delivered with consistency.

Arizcuren.zin: Arizcuren makes nine wines, all red: a village blend called Monte Gatún, six varietal wines (two Mazuelos, two Garnachas, a Graciano and a Maturana), three of which are vinified in amphorae, and two single-parcel wines, called Barranco del Prado and Finca El Foro.
‘That’s why we try to emphasise elegance and subtlety in our wines.’ Arizcuren thinks that Rioja is living through an important period of change.

Artuke.zin: But there’s also a lot happening on the red front in Rioja, with ever more character in site-specific wines (Artuke’s La Condenada) and daring explorations of fruit purity, as found in Ramón Bilbao’s concrete-fermented and long-aged (100 months) Garnacha.
The basic wine, simply called Artuke, is still made as it was in 1991 (and long before that), and is one of the best-value reds in Rioja.

Bodegas Valdemar.zin: A much bigger problem is that, with a handful of exceptions – Castillo de Cuzcurrita’s Tilo, Bodegas Valdemar’s Finca Alto Cantabria and Ostatu’s Gloria de Ostatu – the owners of Rioja’s best sites have not applied to join this particular club.

Carlos Sánchez.zin: There was of course no shortage of gems on the red front; we were blown away by the transparency and nuance of Carlos Sánchez’s La Bendecida and Miguel Merino’s La Quinta Cruz (which also makes the strongest of cases for the potential of the Mazuelo variety).

Juan Carlos Sancha.zin: These are all serious operations, as are the likes of Bodegas Palacio, Juan Carlos Sancha, Luis Cañas, Marqués de Riscal and Dominio de Berzal among the 94 on the existing list.

Miguel Merino.zin: Terroir is essential to our project.’ There are two lines at Miguel Merino – a classic one consisting of a reserva and gran reserva – and a more modern range that’s less dependent on new oak.
His son, Miguel Merino Navajas, is making some of the finest wines in Rioja, and the pride was glowing in his father’s features.

Remírez de Ganuza.zin: Abel Mendoza’s Viura and Remírez de Ganuza’s Olagar show why white Rioja is carving out its place alongside white Burgundy, while López de Haro’s Rosado shows that it’s possible for a wine to be elegant while also being utterly delicious.

Viñedos de Páganos.zin: ‘A bad vineyard is still a bad vineyard,’ says Marcos Eguren at Viñedos de Páganos and Sierra Cantabria, ‘no matter how old it is.’ And a few are waiting to see how the wines are received in the marketplace.

Argyros.zin: Crafted by long-established family winery Argyros, using primarily Assyrtiko from 200-year-old vines rooted in volcanic soils on Santorini, this luscious yet balanced 2015 surely has many decades ahead of it.

Oeno P.zin: Ambitious projects such as Oeno P, that aim to elevate the status of the country’s indigenous grapes and winemaking, are important steps to ensure that Greek Assyrtiko is one day mentioned in the same breath as white Burgundy or Alsatian Riesling.
Given the quality and artisanal nature of these wines – at 20,000 bottles a year Oeno P is a tenth of the production of Domaine Sigalas – I think these prices are justified.

Olianas.zin: On our island, Olianas is carrying out admirable work in this direction.’ Founded by oenologist Stefano Casadei and the Olianas family in 2002, the winery has its headquarters in Gergei, the agricultural-pastoral heart of Sardinia.

Château Climens.zin: And for once, yields were good, with Château Climens reporting 21hl/ha.

Château Gilette.zin: The appellation of the vintage though has to go to Sauternes – and I strongly recommend a jaw-dropping Château Gilette, that was only released on to the market in 2018 and is just a brilliant wine.

Château Lafaurie-Peyraguey.zin: At Château Lafaurie-Peyraguey, the new ownership (since 2013) has also reduced time in barrel and adopted a lighter toast.

Occhipinti.zin: The quest for finesse By making some of the brightest and juiciest wines in Italy, Arianna Occhipinti’s success stems, in part, from her unique ability to defy the stereotypes that Sicilian reds are simply hearty and jammy.

Encouraged by her uncle, Giusto Occhipinti, who had co-founded the renowned COS estate, she established a garage winery, relying on rudimentary equipment and embracing a minimalist philosophy from day one.

Anakota.zin: For Anakota, it’s a tale of two terroirs: the Montana Vineyard, at about 24 hectares, is predominately sandstone and volcanic ash, while the Dakota Vineyard, a mere 4.8 hectares, attributes the red hue of its soils to the high iron content.

Aperture Cellars.zin: This was evident in several wines from Aperture Cellars in Alexander Valley and Williams Selyem in the Russian River Valley, where savoury elements and nuanced complexity stood out over pure fruit notes.

Far Mountain.zin: ‘When Mai (Errazuriz) and I decided to start Far Mountain, we had the opportunity to design our wines from places that felt special to us, with positive energy, surrounded by nature in remote locations with elevation and volcanic rocky soils as the driver,’ says Rodrigo Soto.

Kamen Estate Wines.zin: Credit: Kamen Estate Wines Mountain geology Both tectonic plate shifts and volcanic eruptions formed the Mayacamas Mountain range, where the Moon Mountain AVA sits.

Korbin Kameron.zin: The Kamen Heritage clone is the backbone or “foundational colour,” if you will, of these Moon Mountain District wines.’ Korbin Kameron Wines Korbin Kameron Wine’s proprietor is Korbin Ming, whose parents bought the 8ha property in 1999.
Robert Pepi was Korbin Kameron’s original winemaker, but now Ming, with consulting winemaker Timothy Milos, leads the winemaking with a site-first approach.

Littorai.zin: At Littorai, some sites were picked before or through the heatwave, while others were deliberately held back.

Moon Hollow.zin: Animals are so important to Moon Hollow Ranch that they’re featured on the labels.

Peay Vineyards.zin: In that sense, value can really be found at any price,’ explains Andy Peay, Marketing and Sales Director at Peay Vineyards in the West Sonoma Coast, before adding that ‘it all comes down to quality,’ which, ironically, is another topic that’s up for debate.

Ridge Vineyards.zin: David Gates of Ridge Vineyards notes that diversity in the vineyard fosters resilience because different varieties contribute different strengths.
Known for its pre-industrial agricultural approach, California’s Ridge Vineyards produces estate-grown field blends starring Zinfandel.

Ryme Cellars.zin: Ryme Cellars, for example, has been producing it for years now, successfully keeping the price impressively low for what it offers – under $30 a bottle.

Stonestreet.zin: Credit: Skipstone Stonestreet Estate Vineyards ‘I think people who truly understand Sonoma County world-class expression, Bordeaux varieties, understand that in many cases, time is your ally,’ says second-generation proprietor of Stonestreet Estate Vineyards Chris Jackson.

Williams Selyem.zin: Joseph Swann, Rochioli and Williams Selyem were pivotal early producers here, as was the sparkling wine house Iron Horse.

Adegas Galegas.zin: His Adegas Galegas Veigadares 2017 has a backbone of Albariño – sourced from three separate plots in the sub-regions of Salnes Valley, Condado do Tea and O Rosal.

Albamar.zin: Apart from Señorío de Rubios, other red producers to look out for are Albamar, Attis, Zárate and especially Forjas del Salnés, where Rodri Méndez works with Bierzo superstar Raúl Pérez.

Emilio Rojo.zin: Emilio Rojo, Ribeiro 2015 This is the joy of blind tasting – suddenly encountering an astonishing wine!

Forjas del Salnes.zin: Forjas del Salnes If anyone qualifies as a cult winemaker in Rías Baixas, then it’s arguably self-effacing Rodri Méndez, who has benefited from the advice of Bierzo’s superstar producer, Raúl Pérez, when it comes to his reds (Goliardo is a total bargain).

Martín Códax.zin: Katia Alvarez, winemaker at Martín Códax, began producing a lees-aged Albariño – Martín Códax Lías – in 2005.
She explains that for her the Martín Códax Lías 2018 typifies Rías Baixas.

Pazo Tizón.zin: Pazo Tizón, Extramundi, Ribeiro 2016 I was really excited when this wine was revealed: I’ve loved it since tasting the first vintage, and great to see a top Ribera del Duero producer behind it.

Pazo de Señoráns.zin: However it was the final wine of the tasting, a library vintage of Pazo de Señoráns Selección de Añada 2010, that really stood out in terms of complexity.

Raúl Pérez.zin: With family roots firmly in Spain’s remote northwestern Bierzo region, Raúl Pérez’s minimal-intervention methods and their extraordinary results have rapidly propelled him to the status of global champion.
Raúl Pérez is the archetype of the intuitive winemaking genius.

Domaine Cauhapé.zin: Domaine Cauhapé and Clos Lapèyre are two of the leading producers.

Domaine Rotier.zin: The finest producer here is Domaine Rotier, with Alain Rotier being one of the key winemakers driving the rise in quality of one of Gaillac’s exclusive varieties – Len de l’El (aka Loin de l’Oeil).

Mas del Périé.zin: Mas del Périé produces wines with immediacy and freshness, combined with depth of colour and lingering purity.

Altesino.zin: Short-term pleasure Altesino Upfront in its attractions and should be enjoyed when all of these are in their exuberant prime.

Antinori.zin: One of the first was Antinori, whose 1971 Tignanello was a Sangiovese and Cabernet Sauvignon blend from the Chianti Classico subzone, but declassified to Vino da Tavola.
Antinori’s new bottlings are truly exciting – I was particularly impressed with the San Sano from Gaiole.

Argiano.zin: At Argiano, CEO and winemaker, Bernardino Sani noted the long ripening period between veraison and maturation, describing the resulting grapes as ‘rich in concentration, fruit and colour’.
At Argiano, Bernardino Sani’s greatest concern was ensuring the wine didn’t tire during the long maturation in wood.

Baricci.zin: Then there is Baricci’s Nello, which seems wholly laden with fruit until a complex structure matrix takes hold.

Belguardo.zin: President of the Maremma Toscana consorzio Francesco Mazzei is spearheading the Superiore initiative with his family’s Belguardo estate, releasing V 2021 (formerly ‘Codice V’) as one of the first wines to be labelled Vermentino Superiore.

Bertinga.zin: Bertinga’s Volta di Bertinga and La Massa’s Asiram – both made under the supervision of legendary Bordeaux winemaker Stéphane Derenoncourt – show a UGA-like connection to the sub-zone of origin.

Biondi-Santi.zin: Most of the 2020 Riserva are overshadowed by Le Chiuse and Biondi-Santi’s stellar late-release Riservas – 2016 and 2019 respectively – but my top two picks come from the 2020 vintage, from opposite sides of the region characterised by very different terroirs.

Boscarelli.zin: Michaela’s favourite newly released Vino Nobile di Montepulciano Boscarelli, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano 2019: Fleshy, chewy, racy and nuanced – simply one of the best straight up Vino Nobiles I have tasted.
Nevertheless, there were some pleasant surprises, and both Boscarelli and Dei even managed to capture Sangiovese’s beautiful aromatic intricacies.

Caccia al Piano.zin: I Greppi is worthy of attention due to improved vineyard management, while Caccia al Piano is now bottling their Bolgheri Superiore exclusively from the outstanding vineyard of San Biagio, close to the historical vineyard of Sassicaia.

Caiarossa.zin: Syrah and Cabernet Franc are the key varieties of Caiarossa, a trailblazing wine that embodies the prevailing urge to pursue distinctiveness even when bringing together different grapes in blends.

Canalicchio di Sopra.zin: Standout Brunello 2018 Canalicchio di Sopra Despite a striking new bottling from Montosoli, it was the estate’s classic Brunello that I was particularly taken with.
Both Padelletti and Canalicchio di Sopra were among those who harvested mid- to late-September – essentially the same timing as in other recent vintages.

Capanna.zin: Capanna and Padelletti are more elegantly sculpted yet still decidedly firm.

Capezzana.zin: Of the 20 or so producers in this small, 116-hectare DOCG, Tenuta di Capezzana – owned by the Contini Bonacossi family – is at the top of the heap.

Caprili.zin: Caprili Giacomo Bartolommei is one of Montalcino’s bright young winemakers with a clear vision of the region’s future.

Casanova di Neri.zin: ‘You really felt this in the north,’ says Gianlorenzo Neri at Casanova di Neri, where he cites temperatures of 29°C in the day versus 14 to 15°C at night.

Castagnoli.zin: In the UGA of Castellina, Castagnoli has finally brought its top bottling into the Chianti Classico fold.
Tim Schefenacker at Castagnoli added that there were five days in July that reached 43°C.

Castello Banfi.zin: Meanwhile, Castello Banfi’s 2004 is the best Brunello I’ve tried from the Mariani family for its punch, typicity, accessibility and staying power.

Castello Romitorio.zin: Other wines built along graceful lines are Castello Romitorio, Tassi’s Giuseppe Tassi, Talenti and Val di Suga.

Castello di Ama.zin: Notable exceptions include Castello di Ama’s 2020 single-vineyard La Casuccia and Bellavista bottlings – the latter is one of two wines which received my highest score of the entire Chianti Classico report this year.
The 2020 Bellavista Gran Selezione from Castello di Ama is Michaela Morris’ joint-top scoring Chianti Classico release in 2024.

Castello di Monsanto.zin: Castello di Monsanto: This renowned estate shows a steady progression across Chianti Classico’s three categories in the 2016, 2017 and 2018 vintages.

Col di Lamo.zin: Other smaller, and essentially brand new, estates such as Gianna Neri’s Col di Lamo and the Terzuoli family’s SassodiSole in Montalcino’s still very unfashionable Torrenieri showed no newcomers’ nerves.

Cortonesi.zin: Cortonesi, La Mannella In Montalcino’s northern sector, La Mannella has been improving steadily over the years.

Donne Fittipaldi.zin: Donne Fittipaldi’s ‘Magnetic’ Bolgheri Rosso (Cabernet Franc aged in amphorae and cocciopesto) is a benchmark in this regard.

Fattoi.zin: Fattoi A perennial pick, Fattoi is among my favourite wines of the vintage not just for the exceptional value it represents, but also for its palpable sense of place.
Giodo is one of my top picks for the second year in a row and Fattoi joins the ranks, not just for the sheer value it represents but for its palpable sense of place.

Fattoria dei Barbi.zin: Historic estates in the warmer south like Fattoria dei Barbi and Ciacci Piccolomini showed the value of old school winemaking practises, guiding rather than dictating ferments, leading to open-knit Brunellos whose soft autumnal flavours flow.

Fontodi.zin: Fontodi’s Vigna del Sorbo is particularly emblematic but executes this with unbelievable refinement.

Fuligni.zin: Standout Brunello producers in 2016: Fuligni produced the top wine for me in 2016 – elegant in its power with great complexity and the vintage’s radiant acidity.

Gianni Brunelli.zin: Gianni Brunelli Pretty fragrances, freshness and deftly managed tannins are among the highlights of this estate’s 2017.

Giuseppe Gorelli.zin: Mid-term appeal Giuseppe Gorelli Third vintage is a charm for this new winery.

Guado al Tasso.zin: Guado al Tasso takes this to the next level by using Vermentino clones from Corsica, which I’m told have more aromatic potential than the traditional Tuscan Vermentino.
At Guado al Tasso, new plantings are trained higher off the ground to allow more air to circulate and prevent diseases such as peronospera.

Il Marroneto.zin: Il Marroneto Alessandro Mori’s Madonna delle Grazie is one of the top wines of the vintage and his estate bottling isn’t far behind.

Il Molinaccio.zin: Il Molinaccio, La Spinosa, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano 2019: From a cool pocket of Montepulciano, this is textured, crunchy and pure with huge drinkability.
Marco Malavasi at Il Molinaccio concurs, asserting that ‘2018 was a good year but not good enough to produce a Riserva.’ How do the Vino Nobile 2018s taste?

Il Molino di Grace.zin: Bibbiano’s Vigna del Capannino allows a sense of place to shine through, and in Il Molino di Grace’s predominantly new barrique-aged Il Margone, the wood is well-integrated.
From Panzano, where Pietraforte (a hard, calcareous sandstone) abounds, Il Molino di Grace and Fontodi’s 2021s are deeply coloured, darkly fruited and amply structured.

Il Poggione.zin: ‘You had to pick around the rains,’ recalls Francesca Bindocci at Il Poggione, adding that it’s a vintage which shows who worked well in the vineyard throughout the year.
Value picks Il Poggione (95): With a production of 200,000 bottles, this is an excellent ambassador for the region and vintage.

Isola delle Falcole.zin: Equally notable is Isola delle Falcole’s fifth-ever vintage from a vineyard in the wilds of Panzano.

Isole e Olena.zin: Isole e Olena’s excellent 2021 is all this – with extra tautness.

Istine.zin: Vigna Istine and Vigna Cavarchione (respectively from Radda and Gaiole) are among my top wines of the vintage and clearly belong at the apex of Chianti Classico’s pyramid.
I was also privy to a stunning sneak peek of Istine’s collection, which includes two new Gran Selezione – one from Lamole and the other from Vagliagli.

La Montanina.zin: Top achievers, such as Poggerino, Monteraponi’s Il Campitello and La Montanina have the potential for 15 years in the cellar.

La Vigna di San Martino ad Argiano.zin: Furthermore, boutique producer, Maurizio Alongi and promising newcomer, La Vigna di San Martino ad Argiano have selected the Riserva category for the sole Chianti Classico each produces.

Le Chiuse.zin: ‘It was hard to make bad Brunello in 2019,’ Le Chiuse’s Lorenzo Magnelli declared – and yet, some did.
Le Chiuse Lorenzo Magnelli has managed to coax the very best from the challenging 2017 vintage.

Le Cinciole.zin: Completing my selection of 90 annata recommendations are half a dozen new releases from 2021, with Le Cinciole and I Fabbri’s Terra di Lamole particularly of note, as well as the excellent 2020 Castell’in Villa.
Nevertheless, it has encouraged Orsini to upgrade Le Cinciole’s Aluigi bottling from Riserva to Gran Selezione with the just released, excellent 2016.

Le Crocine.zin: In 2016, Marzichi Lenzi released his first Bolgheri Superiore, Le Crocine’s 57022, which is one of the top wines in its lower price range given his almost exclusively local reputation.
Aldo’s Bolgheri 2016 best value picks: Le Crocine, 57022, Bolgheri Superiore 2016 Le Crocine is one of Bolgheri’s newest additions.

Le Mortelle.zin: This year celebrating the 50th anniversary of the launch of Tignanello, Antinori has conducted thorough experiments at Le Mortelle in coastal Maremma, where the pivot is Cabernet Franc for Poggio alle Nane and Carmenère for Ampio.

Le Potazzine.zin: In a not dissimilar stylistic vein was Tenuta Le Potazzine, made by duo Gigliola Giannetti and Giuseppe Gorelli, the latter a Montalcino-based winemaking consultant.
Le Potazzine While almost impossibly embryonic now, it is showing just enough to reassure of a long and lively future.

Le Ragnaie.zin: Le Ragnaie Riccardo Campinoti’s Casanovina Montosoli is the finest of his solid 2017 lineup.
Riccardo Campinoti (Le Ragnaie), however, recalls that ‘there weren’t big problems’.

Lisini.zin: In the case of Lisini’s promising new wine, Poggio Severo is a direct response to the changing climate.

Masseto.zin: Today, carved into the ancient blue clay that makes up the vineyard, the Masseto winery is a physical and symbolic tribute to the estate’s history and rapid evolution, from a humble intuition about the hidden potential of a vineyard site to an internationally acclaimed wine.

We worked with extraction to manage the concentration,’ says Gaia Cinnirella, Masseto’s winemaker, explaining that during the 2023 harvest period, they tasted the grapes in the vineyards every day, and picked plot by plot.

Mastrojanni.zin: Mastrojanni, Vigna Schiena d’Asino As hard as it is to resist now, this will reveal the full range of its complexities for years to come.

Monte Bernardi.zin: Monte Bernardi was down a whopping 80%, whereas Le Cinciole estimates a more modest shortfall of 10-15%, for example.

Montecalvi.zin: There were the necessary treatments against mildew but as Tim Manning at Montecalvi in Greve reported, ‘disease pressure was low.’ Summer was long and hot without significant heat spikes and it cooled off sufficiently at night.

Monteraponi.zin: Particularly impressive was Monteraponi’s first ever Gran Selezione – ‘Il Bragantino’ – which sits alongside Bellavista at the top of my rankings.

Mulini di Segalari.zin: Mulini di Segalari, Ai Confini del Bosco, Bolgheri 2016 Ai Confini del Bosco, from the Mulini di Segalari estate, is possibly the least costly wine in Bolgheri (€16-18 RRP).

Ornellaia.zin: The older vintages Marco chooses to open at both Ornellaia and Masseto are years with similar conditions to 2021 and – in the case of Ornellaia – similar blends, yet the refinement of the winemaking process from then to now is striking.

Ornellaia was one of the first Italian wineries to employ Simonit & Sirch, who pioneered a way of pruning that has since caught on among some of the most revered estates in the world – as well as ambitious smaller estates.

Padelletti.zin: Le Chiuse and Padelletti are more finely framed but not lacking depth.

Petrolo.zin: Monteraponi’s Trebbiano, first bottled in 2012 from vines in Radda in Chianti, and Petrolo’s Bòggina B, first produced in 2014 from clones of 1970s plantings in Valdarno di Sopra, are both fundamental to Trebbiano Toscano’s comeback.

Podere Poggio Scalette.zin: Exemplifying this are wines like Bibbiano, Podere Poggio Scalette and Montesecondo.

Poggerino.zin: In Radda, Poggerino’s Piero Lanza had to bring in fruit from more humid plots early – in mid-September – due to the threat of botrytis and acid rot.
Poggerino opted to forgo a Riserva selection this year, to the benefit of the estate’s annata, which is among my top value picks.

Poggio al Tesoro.zin: Poggio al Tesoro, Il Seggio, Bolgheri 2016 Il Seggio, awarded a Platinum medal at last year’s Decanter World Wine Awards, is the entry-level wine of Poggio al Tesoro, the Allegrini family’s estate in Bolgheri.

Poggio di Sotto.zin: The 2017 annata still captures Poggio di Sotto’s style and the 2016 Riserva is worthy of its category.
Poggio di Sotto Shorter macerations and less time in wood than usual were wise decisions here.

Poliziano.zin: The Consorzio awarded the vintage five stars, and Poliziano’s Federico Carletti calls it ‘one of the best in the last 10 years.’ Vintage conditions In stark contrast to the cool and rainy 2014 vintage, the growing season in 2015 was hot and sunny.

Querciabella.zin: Along with Istine’s inaugual Elle bottling is Fontodi’s newest offering, Pastrolo, and Querciabella’s Gran Selezione now includes fruit from recently acquired holdings there.
While the dry, hot 2017 vintage was a challenge, Querciabella managed to find balance and was unanimously noted as having the stuffing and framework to make it cellarworthy.

Rocca di Montegrossi.zin: According to Marco Ricasoli-Firidolfi at Rocca di Montegrossi in Gaiole, ‘from Christmas of 2019 until the end of May, precipitation was a rare occurrence.’ Temperatures, nevertheless, were cool and late spring brought adequate rainfall that replenished reserves.

Salcheto.zin: Though not dissatisfied with the vintage, Michele Manelli at Salcheto admits to being a bit squeezed, saying that the vines never completely caught up after the cooler temperatures early in the summer.
See all of our Tuscany vintage reports Salcheto winemaker Michele Manelli emphasises the warmth of the vintage.

Salicutti.zin: ‘We were concerned about mildew but the northern wind dried the grapes well.’ Conversely, Salicutti reported losing production of the estate’s Teatro vineyard, despite working ‘meticulously’.

San Filippo.zin: Brunello 2018 for the cellar San Filippo, La Lucère One of my top wines of the vintage, La Lucère has reached an extraordinary level of elegance without sacrificing substance and structure for ageing.

San Giusto a Rentennano.zin: Finally, from one of the region’s warmer pockets, San Giusto a Rentennano’s 2022 Le Baròncole is impressive.

San Polino.zin: Further south, the Loacker family’s Corte Pavone and San Polino were especially notable for being among the very few certified organic or biodynamic estates in Montalcino in 2004.
San Polino’s conscientious vineyard practises surpass organic and biodynamic protocols, and the wines are expressively pure Sangiovese.

San Polo.zin: San Polo Marilisa Allegrini’s Montalcino property has gone from strength to strength since the arrival of winemaker Riccardo Fratton in 2015, with the introduction of two single-vineyard bottlings the same year and organic certification as of 2017.
At San Polo, the winery’s two single vineyards are side by side.

Talenti.zin: According to Riccardo Talenti (Talenti), whose vineyards are in the south, deciding when to pick was the most challenging aspect of the year.
Talenti Has all the estate’s signature fragrance and texture; just ready to go a bit sooner than usual.

Tenuta Gracciano della Seta.zin: What to buy After tasting the wines blind, my top 2015s were Metinella, Tenuta Gracciano della Seta, Avignonesi and Poliziano’s Asinone.

Tenuta San Guido.zin: The 2018 Sassicaia is the 50th edition officially produced by Tenuta San Guido (although the marquise has bottled it since 1948).

Tenuta Trerose.zin: Boscarelli has coaxed out admirable elegance, and Tenuta Trerose charms with its succulence.

Tenuta di Arceno.zin: Further north in the district, Tenuta di Arceno is gentler in expression owing in part to vineyards on non-calcareous sandstone soil known as ‘macigno ‘.

Terreno.zin: Terreno, Sillano, Chianti Classico Gran Selezione 2019: The first ever vintage of this single-vineyard selection from up-and-comer, Sofia Ruhne is a stunner.
On Macigno (non-calcareous sandstone) soil conversely, Terreno’s 2020 Asofia caresses with softer, finer tannins, though is not lacking in a plush core.

Tua Rita.zin: ‘It shines for its versatility,’ notes D’Attoma, who worked with prominent Suvereto estate Tua Rita to craft Keir, the most groundbreaking among at least a dozen new-wave Syrahs fermenting in Tuscan terracotta amphorae.

Val di Suga.zin: Val di Suga, a single site specialist, produced a beautifully fresh Brunello from its Spuntali vineyard.

Valdicava.zin: For Vincenzo Abbruzzese at Valdicava, who calls 2019 ‘a fairy-tale vintage with an American ending,’ the only challenge was sacrificing 2018.

Bertani.zin: And there are technical reasons for that: since the foundation of the estate in Quinto di Valpantena, the Bertani brothers put to use what they had learned about viticulture and winemaking from the legendary French expert, Jules Guyot.

This cru (along with another, called ‘Le Miniere’) reflects Bertani’s desire to showcase the region’s terroir, and the audience’s positive reaction to the wine would indicate that it clearly has a place in the market.

Brigaldara.zin: Cautious about declaring blanket success, Antonio Cesari at Brigaldara describes 2016 as ‘a year for growers and terroir’.

Buglioni.zin: Buglioni’s 44 Verticale Classico Superiore 2019 is a good example.

Gentili.zin: I particularly appreciate the interpretation of Bardolino by Gentili winery.’ Bardolino is a misunderstood red, despite being produced with the same grapes as Amarone.

Massimago.zin: Here are five worth knowing: Cà La Bionda Campagnola’s Caterina Zardini estate Massimago Mont’Albano Novaia Five great value Amarone Affordable for more relaxed drinking, or a little more expensive but well worth the extra – here are five great value Amarone.

Roccolo Grassi.zin: In the words of Marco Sartori, owner-winemaker at the Roccolo Grassi estate, ‘It was not a classic vintage’.

Romano Dal Forno.zin: Nature and nurture Romano Dal Forno’s Amarone is sourced from a single vineyard in the Illasi Valley, called Monte Lodoletta, located at an altitude of around 300 metres on the flatter mid-slope, overlooked by the modern winery (completed at the end of 2007).
Evolution Romano Dal Forno’s earliest vintages are really interesting, as you can almost envisage him dialling everything in as he learns.

Serego Alighieri.zin: Masi’s Amarone crus Serego Alighieri, Vaio Armaron, Amarone della Valpolicella Classico This vineyard selection comes from the estate of Serego Alighieri at Sant’Ambrogio, which Masi has managed since 1973.

Tedeschi.zin: There were those from Speri, Tedeschi and Tommasi – deeply coloured, firmly structured, with more grip to the tannins and with darker flavours and aromas.
Recchia, Begali and Tedeschi’s Ansari lean towards the former, while Montresor, Pasqua and Cà La Bionda are in the more modern style.

Venturini.zin: For example, I found Venturini’s Riserva 2001 to be showing beautifully now, while some 2011s were already looking tired.

Adega de Monção.zin: Adega de Monção One of Portugal’s top cooperatives, founded in the 1950s, when best-selling Alvarinho brand, Deu La Deu, was created.

Aphros.zin: Aphros’ sophisticated Vinhấo range includes a Palhete (the term refers to wines made by co-fermenting red and white grapes; here Vinhão has been fermented with a small percentage of Loureiro) made in amphora under the Phaunus label.
Aphros ‘Ouranus’ is one of a new breed of ‘glou glou’ (gluggable) wines.

Pequenos Rebentos.zin: Signposting artisanal trends, micro-negociant Márcio Lopes sources sappy red Pequenos Rebentos Atlântico (a Cainho-Alvarelhão-Pedral blend) from ramada vines (which Sem Igual are also exploring).
His Pequenos Rebentos Selvagem, on the other hand, is an amphora-fermented, barrel-aged Azal from traditional enforcado vines.

Quinta de Azevedo.zin: However, susceptible to disease and botrytis in the Atlantic-influenced Cávado sub-region, Quinta de Azevedo’s Arinto has been replaced with Loureiro, which António Braga finds ‘a much better terroir fit’.

Quinta de Soalheiro.zin: Fifty producers (and many more growers) account for 70% of Portugal’s Alvarinho plantings, according to Quinta de Soalheiro’s genial chief winemaker, António Luís Cerdeira (‘Luís’), who is proud of Monção e Melgaço’s special microclimate.

Quinta de Soalheiro Home to Melgaço’s first Alvarinho vineyard (1974), the dynamic second generation makes a range of twelve expressions of the variety, from certified organic estate and grower grapes.

Quinta do Ameal.zin: Having led Vinho Verde’s quality charge together with Soalheiro, Quinta do Ameal and Aphros, the winemaker is delighted about receiving recognition from big Portuguese players.

Sem Igual.zin: Sem Igual made a textural, rounded, ageworthy example until 2016, when it blended Azal with Arinto for a fresher style.
Sem Igual True to the label (meaning ‘without equal’), João and Leila Camizão’s label is about differentiation.

Cadence.zin: But it fits our style, a little more acidity, and the tannins aren’t quite so soft.’ Cadence at a glance Established: Cadence was established in 1998 after Ben Smith left his career at Boeing.
According to the team at Cadence, the physical makeup of the cobbles and clay is similar to the Pomerol and St-Emilion plateau in Bordeaux.

Quilceda Creek.zin: It’s a classic vintage for Quilceda Creek – the wines have tremendous concentration and depth.’ ‘Overall, the 2020s offer a bit of extra concentration from the low yields,’ said Delille’s Jason Gorski.
Quilceda Creek wines from this site are known for their pillowy soft dark fruit profiles with a weightless texture, as well as tar, tobacco, sagebrush and chocolate undertones.

Syncline.zin: There are small producers like Syncline located in the cooler Columbia Gorge that have made sparkling wines for a long time.

Trothe.zin: Part of crafting a wine like Trothe is a hope to transport people, if even for a moment, to the sagebrush-covered canyons and windswept ridges of the wide-open Horse Heaven Hills.’ ‘Trothe is part of our family’s continuing farming and wine-growing evolution,’ Andrews continues.

This block will become more prominent in the Trothe blend over the next 10-15 years as the vines grow up and settle into their terroir.’ Rugged beauty Many parts of Washington’s wine country can be surprising for the uninitiated.

WT Vintners.zin: Jeff Lindsay-Thorsen, MS of WT Vintners, whose Boushey Vineyard Syrah was among the top three wines in my vintage report, makes wines in the $50 and under category as a rule.

Alheit Vineyards.zin: Chris Alheit of Alheit Vineyards says that Chenin is less forgiving than some people imagine – the picking window can be as narrow as two days in some sites – and that the best examples need to be handled like any fine wine.

Boschkloof.zin: Natural progression In Boschkloof’s cellar, the use of new oak has been drastically brought down, with open-top concrete and larger oak vessels favoured for vinifying multiple components separately.

Botanica.zin: Even a famous grower such as Henk Laing, who sells to Botanica Wines, Fram and Savage from his farm on the West Coast, says, ‘I couldn’t survive from selling grapes alone’.

Ken Forrester.zin: Ken Forrester’s The FMC – a self-confident attempt to ‘make the best wine in the world and sell it at the same price as a top Chardonnay’ – was released in 2000, two years after its eponymous owner had founded the Chenin Blanc Association of South Africa.

toelichting: Eén of twee zinnen per wijnhuis uit de lopende tekst van Decanters jaargangs- en proefverslagen. Een zin over de streek zegt iets over duizend wijnen; een zin over het domein zegt iets over de fles in je hand. Alleen huizen waarvan hetzelfde artikel ook een wijn toont tellen mee: dat sluit toevallige naamgelijkenis uit, want San Polo is in Montalcino ook een gehucht. Weggegooid zijn navigatie- en nieuwsbriefteksten, opsommingen van drie of meer namen, zinnen zonder werkwoord en zinnen die met een kleine letter beginnen: van 2680 geoogste zinnen bleven er 1385 over. De proefnotities van Decanter zitten achter hun betaalmuur en hun scores zijn afbeeldingen; hier staat alleen publiek geserveerde lopende tekst, en geen enkel cijfer.
